title: ii. dreams in the key of godhead — ron takes notes

nodes.text: ii. dreams in the key of godhead — ron takes notes
Ron catches me on the stairs after supper and asks if I've got an hour. He asks like he already knows.
His room is how Betty said. Books on the floor in drifts, dust in the lamplight, nowhere to stand. He clears a spot on the bed for me with his forearm and sits at the desk half turned away.
The typewriter is black and big as an engine block. He rolls in a fresh sheet and squares it and waits.
The page is blank except for the title at the top, centered, underlined twice.
The springs give under me and books slide off the far side of the bed, one, then another.
Where were you, the day before Jack found you on his floor?
I tell him Houston. I tell him a hospital. He doesn't ask what Houston is like now, or what a hospital is like. He asks something else.
What did the air smell like?
Cold. Rubbing alcohol. And something under the alcohol.
He types. Loud, a burst, a pause, a burst. The bell dings at the end of the line and he slaps the carriage back without looking.
And the light?
There were screens over every bed. A green line on each one, going up and down. Little lights all over the machines, blinking. Like eyes.
How many machines?
A whole floor of them. The whole top floor.
Did they fly?
I laugh, first time in I don't know how long, and it hurts like a cough.
The helicopters did. They landed on the roof all night. Bringing people in.
He types a long time on that.
What color were their lights, coming down?
Red and white. When they're both going and it's hazy out, it comes through the blinds pink.
And the ones they carried in, were they awake?
Mostly not.
Who was in the room with him?
I tell him. My mother by the window. My sister, who had to leave for a shot so she could go to Brazil and study rocks the way he did. Me.
And where were you?

I tell him the floor. I tell him I slept next to the air conditioner because I used to do that when I was a kid, the hum. I tell him I slept through the worst of it and woke up when it was almost over. I haven't told anybody that.
I didn't know I was going to say it until it was out in the room with the dust.
Ron doesn't stop typing to look at me. I am grateful to him for that.
Did they have to hold him down?
He tried to get up out of the bed. The drugs had him confused. They strapped him down and he fought them.
Did he say anything?
Not words, by then. He was angry. He sounded like he was begging for something.
Begging for what?
To go home. I think he wanted to go home.
He types. I don't look over his shoulder. I don't want to see what he does with it.
What did your father do?
Geologist. He taught. He took kids out into the field and showed them how to read a road cut. Oil, for a while.
Did he make you study?
He handed me books. Science fiction, mostly. Old paperbacks with the covers falling off.
Were they any good?
No. I read every one of them.
He types that too, or something like it. The bell rings.
And outside the hospital that night, what was the world doing?
Nothing. That's the thing. Cars on the freeway. Planes coming in to land. Everybody going to work in the morning. The world ended on one floor and nobody else got the memo.
He types a long time on that and doesn't ask me anything for a while.
Do you mind?
I tell him no. I tell him take it. Somebody ought to.
How does it end?
He dies, Ron.
And the boy?

I lie back on his bed with the books. The typewriter keeps going, burst and pause and bell. Down the hall Betty is laughing at something Jack said. The window is open and the air comes in heavy with oranges.
Ron asks me something else. I'm most of the way asleep by then and I don't catch it.
